import "core/ord.ct"
import "core/functor.ct"
import "core/monad.ct"


module(Data)
  # # Lists
    A [List] is an ordered collection of zero or more items. [List] is an interface: it names the
    operations every list supports without fixing how the items are stored. Concrete list types
    implement it — this file provides the [ConsList], and a future [ArrayList] or [TreeList] would
    be another. Because [sum], [reversed], [sorted] and the rest are declared on [List] rather than
    on one concrete type, every list type reuses those same declarations just by being a [List]. The
    [List] interface lives here directly under [Data]; the [ConsList] implementation and the
    operations all live in the [Data/List] namespace it opens.
  class(List[$T])

# # The ConsList and the List operations
  Everything else list-related lives in [module(Data/List)] — the namespace the [List] class opens —
  so the [ConsList] type, its constructors [Cons]/[Nil], and every operation sit under [/Data/List]
  rather than loose at the top of [/Data].
module(Data/List)
  class(ConsList[$T], [Cons[$T -> $_T](head -> $T, tail -> ConsList[$T -> $_T]), Nil])
    # A [ConsList] is the simplest [List]: either empty ([Nil]) or an item ([head]) prepended to a
      smaller list ([tail]). Almost every operation below is a two-arm recursion — a base case for
      [Nil], and a step that consumes the [head] and recurses on the [tail].

  every(ConsList[$T -> $_T], isa= [/Data/List[$T -> $_T]])
    # Every [ConsList] is a [List], so each [List] operation resolves on it through the arms below.

  # ## Bracket syntax
    The literal [[1, 2, 3]] is sugar for a [ConsList]: it expands to [Cons(1, Cons(2, Cons(3,
    Nil)))], and [[]] is [Nil]. The examples throughout this file use it.
  # ## Length
  :/Data/List.length -> Integer
    # The number of items in a list, found by walking to the end. It is declared on [List] (any
      list has a length) and implemented here for the [ConsList] constructors.
  :Nil.length= 0
  Cons(head, tail).length= 1 + tail.length
  :/Data/List.length -> Integer_nonNeg
    # A length is never negative — a refinement the derived agreement tests check against the
      definition above.
    #refine

  > [10, 20, 30].length
    >>> 3
  # ## Folds
    [foldr] collapses a list from the right: every [Cons] becomes a step function and the [Nil]
    becomes an initial value, so [foldr(lst= [a, b], fn, init)] is [fn(acc= fn(acc= init, v= b), v=
    a)]. The accumulator carries its own type variable, so the answer need not be the element type —
    the examples fold [Integer]s into an [Integer] and into a [String]. The step is passed onward as
    [fn(acc, v)= fn(acc= acc, v= v)] rather than bare, the re-wrap every higher-order argument needs
    (see [Data/bind]).
  foldr[$A, $B](lst -> /Data/List[$T -> $_A], fn(acc -> $_B, v -> $_A) -> $_B, init -> $_B) -> $_B
  foldr(lst= Nil, fn(acc, v), init)= init
  foldr(lst= Cons(head, tail), fn(acc, v), init)= fn(acc= foldr(lst= tail, fn(acc, v)= fn(acc= acc, v= v), init= init), v= head)

  > /Data/List/foldr(lst= [1, 2, 3], fn(acc, v)= acc + v, init= 0)
    >>> 6
  > /Data/List/foldr(lst= [], fn(acc, v)= acc + v, init= 0)
    >>> 0
  > /Data/List/foldr(lst= [1, 2], fn(acc, v)= acc ++ "x", init= "s")
    >>> sxx
  # [foldl] collapses from the left instead, carrying the accumulator forward as it walks, so
    [foldl(lst= [a, b], fn, init)] is [fn(acc= fn(acc= init, v= a), v= b)]. The two agree when the
    step is associative and differ when it is not, which the [String] examples show.
  foldl[$A, $B](lst -> /Data/List[$T -> $_A], fn(acc -> $_B, v -> $_A) -> $_B, init -> $_B) -> $_B
  foldl(lst= Nil, fn(acc, v), init)= init
  foldl(lst= Cons(head, tail), fn(acc, v), init)= foldl(lst= tail, fn(acc, v)= fn(acc= acc, v= v), init= fn(acc= init, v= head))

  > /Data/List/foldl(lst= [1, 2, 3], fn(acc, v)= acc + v, init= 0)
    >>> 6
  > /Data/List/foldl(lst= [], fn(acc, v)= acc + v, init= 0)
    >>> 0
  > /Data/List/foldl(lst= [1, 2], fn(acc, v)= acc ++ "x", init= "s")
    >>> sxx
  # TODO: [append] and [reversed] below are folds too and are still their own two-arm recursions.
    [reversed] is a [foldl] with [Cons] as the step, and [append] is what [mmap] is built on, so
    rewriting it moves the whole [Monad] instance with it.
  # ## Summing
  sum(lst -> /Data/List[$T -> Integer]) -> Integer
    # [sum] adds a list of [Integer]s: [foldr] with addition, starting from zero.
  sum(lst)= foldr(lst= lst, fn(acc, v)= acc + v, init= 0)

  > /Data/List/sum(lst= [1, 2, 3])
    >>> 6
  > /Data/List/sum(lst= [])
    >>> 0
  # ## Universal and existential quantifiers
  all(lst -> /Data/List[$T -> Boolean]) -> Boolean
    # [all] is [True] when every element of a list of [Boolean]s is [True]. The empty list is
      vacuously [True], and each element is [and]ed with the result for the rest.
  all(lst)= foldr(lst= lst, fn(acc, v)= acc && v, init= /Data/Primitive/True)

  > /Data/List/all(lst= [True, True])
    >>> True
  > /Data/List/all(lst= [False])
    >>> False
  any(lst -> /Data/List[$T -> Boolean]) -> Boolean
    # [any] is [True] when at least one element is [True] — the mirror of [all], with [or] and a
      [False] base case for the empty list.
  any(lst)= foldr(lst= lst, fn(acc, v)= acc || v, init= /Data/Primitive/False)

  > /Data/List/any(lst= [True])
    >>> True
  > /Data/List/any(lst= [False, False])
    >>> False
  # ## Quantifying over a predicate
    [all] and [any] read a list that already holds [Boolean]s. [allBy] and [anyBy] are the
    higher-order forms: they take the list and a predicate, and ask the question of every element.
    Both are written by [fmap]ping the predicate across the list and handing the resulting
    [Boolean] list to [all]/[any] — the elements never have to be [Boolean] themselves, so these
    work on a list of anything. The predicate is passed onward as [fn(v)= fn(v= v)] rather than
    bare; a bare [fn] does not typecheck (see [Data/bind] for the same re-wrap).
  allBy[$A](lst -> /Data/List/ConsList[$T -> $_A], fn(v -> $_A) -> Boolean) -> Boolean
    # [allBy] is [True] when every element satisfies the predicate, and vacuously [True] for the
      empty list.
  allBy(lst, fn(v))= all(lst= /Data/Functor/fmap(lst= lst, fn(v)= fn(v= v)))

  anyBy[$A](lst -> /Data/List/ConsList[$T -> $_A], fn(v -> $_A) -> Boolean) -> Boolean
    # [anyBy] is [True] when at least one element satisfies the predicate, and [False] for the
      empty list.
  anyBy(lst, fn(v))= any(lst= /Data/Functor/fmap(lst= lst, fn(v)= fn(v= v)))

  > /Data/List/allBy(lst= [1, 2, 3], fn(v)= v > 0)
    >>> True
  > /Data/List/allBy(lst= [1, 2, 3], fn(v)= v > 2)
    >>> False
  > /Data/List/allBy(lst= [], fn(v)= v > 2)
    >>> True
  > /Data/List/anyBy(lst= [1, 2, 3], fn(v)= v > 2)
    >>> True
  > /Data/List/anyBy(lst= [1, 2, 3], fn(v)= v > 9)
    >>> False
  > /Data/List/anyBy(lst= [], fn(v)= v > 0)
    >>> False
  # ## Membership
  elem[$A -> /Data/Algebra/Eq](lst -> /Data/List/ConsList[$T -> $_A], item -> $A) -> Boolean
    # [elem] is [True] when the list holds an element equal to [item]. It is [anyBy] with equality
      as the predicate, so it works for any [Eq] element type rather than one concrete one.
  elem(lst, item)= anyBy(lst= lst, fn(v)= v == item)

  > /Data/List/elem(lst= [1, 2, 3], item= 2)
    >>> True
  > /Data/List/elem(lst= [1, 2, 3], item= 9)
    >>> False
  > /Data/List/elem(lst= [], item= 1)
    >>> False
  # ## Filtering
    [filter] keeps the elements a predicate accepts, in their original order. It is written over
    [mmap]: each element becomes a one-element list where the predicate holds and the empty list
    where it does not, and [mmap] concatenates those — so a rejected element contributes nothing.
    [keepIf] is local to the definition because it is an artifact of that encoding rather than an
    operation a caller would want.
  filter[$A](lst -> ConsList[$T -> $_A], fn(v -> $_A) -> Boolean) -> ConsList[$T -> $_A]
  filter(lst, fn(v)) =
    keepIf(v -> $_A, keep -> Boolean) -> ConsList[$T -> $_A]
    keepIf(v, keep= /Data/Primitive/True)= [v]
    keepIf(v, keep= /Data/Primitive/False)= []

    /Data/Monad/mmap(m= lst, fn(v)= keepIf(v= v, keep= fn(v= v)))

  > /Data/List/filter(lst= [1, 2, 3, 4], fn(v)= v > 2)
    >>> [3, 4]
  > /Data/List/filter(lst= ["ab", "c", "de"], fn(v)= v == "c")
    >>> [c]
  > /Data/List/filter(lst= [], fn(v)= v > 2)
    >>> []
  # ## Counting matches
  count[$A](lst -> ConsList[$T -> $_A], fn(v -> $_A) -> Boolean) -> Integer
    # [count] is how many elements satisfy the predicate: [filter] followed by [length].
  count(lst, fn(v))= filter(lst= lst, fn(v)= fn(v= v)).length

  > /Data/List/count(lst= [1, 2, 3, 4], fn(v)= v > 2)
    >>> 2
  > /Data/List/count(lst= [], fn(v)= v > 2)
    >>> 0
  # ## Missing combinators
    TODO: [concat] — [mmap(m= lst, fn(v)= v)] — still does not compile, and it now fails
    DIFFERENTLY from how it used to. It exhausts memory during TYPE INFERENCE: [catln epochs] on a
    file declaring it passes 8GB of RSS in 70s and never reports, where the same file calling
    [mmap] ordinarily finishes in 36s at 1.0GB over 804 epochs. It previously failed at EVALUATION
    with [catln: <<loop>>]. Since type inference runs before tree building, any diagnosis resting
    on a tree-build-time structure cannot explain the current failure and needs re-deriving.
    The shape to isolate is that [concat] makes the element dimension the same shape as the
    container — [fn(v)= v] forces both the monad variable and the element variable to [ConsList].
  # ## Reversing
  reversed(lst -> /Data/List) -> /Data/List
    # [reversed] returns a list with its items in the opposite order. Since there is no
      list-append operator, it is built with [reverseOnto], which moves items one at a time onto an
      accumulator that starts empty — each [head] is prepended to the growing result, which leaves
      the accumulator holding the reversal once [lst] is exhausted.
  reversed(lst) =
    reverseOnto(lst -> ConsList, acc -> ConsList) -> ConsList
    reverseOnto(lst= Nil, acc)= acc
    reverseOnto(lst= Cons(head, tail), acc)= reverseOnto(lst= tail, acc= Cons(head= head, tail= acc))
    reverseOnto(lst= lst, acc= Nil)

  > /Data/List/reversed(lst= [1, 2, 3])
    >>> [3, 2, 1]
  > /Data/List/reversed(lst= [])
    >>> []
  # ## Sorting
  sorted[$T -> /Data/Algebra/Ord](lst -> /Data/List[$T -> $_T]) -> /Data/List[$T -> $_T]
    # [sorted] returns the items of an [Ord] list in ascending order using insertion sort: it sorts
      the [tail], then [insert]s the [head] into the sorted result. [insert] walks the already
      sorted list and places [x] before the first item it is not greater than — the [x <= head]
      decision is a guard on [insert]'s own arms, so no separate step function holds it.
  sorted(lst= Nil)= Nil
  sorted(lst= Cons[$T -> /Data/Algebra/Ord](head@h, tail@t)) =
    insert[$T -> /Data/Algebra/Ord](x -> $T, lst -> ConsList[$T -> /Data/Algebra/Ord]) -> ConsList[$T -> $_T]
    insert(x, lst= Nil)= Cons(head= x, tail= Nil)
    insert(x, lst= Cons[$T -> /Data/Algebra/Ord](head, tail)) | x.compareTo(other= head).isLessEq= Cons(head= x, tail= Cons(head= head, tail= tail))
    insert(x, lst= Cons[$T -> /Data/Algebra/Ord](head, tail)) else = Cons(head= head, tail= insert(x= x, lst= tail))
    insert(x= h, lst= sorted(lst= t))

  > /Data/List/sorted(lst= [3, 1, 2])
    >>> [1, 2, 3]
  > /Data/List/sorted(lst= [5, 4, 4, 1])
    >>> [1, 4, 4, 5]
  # ## Counting ranges
  range(stop -> Integer) -> /Data/List[$T -> Integer]
    # [range] builds the counting list [[0, 1, ..., stop - 1]]. It counts up from zero with
      [rangeFrom], whose guard carries the [i < stop] decision: while the counter is below [stop] it
      prepends the counter and recurses, and otherwise it stops with [Nil]. A [stop] of zero or less
      yields the empty list.
  range(stop) =
    rangeFrom(i -> Integer, stop -> Integer) -> ConsList[$T -> Integer]
    rangeFrom(i, stop) | i < stop= Cons(head= i, tail= rangeFrom(i= i + 1, stop= stop))
    rangeFrom(i, stop) else = Nil
    rangeFrom(i= 0, stop= stop)

  > /Data/List/range(stop= 3)
    >>> [0, 1, 2]
  > /Data/List/range(stop= 0)
    >>> []
  # ## Rendering as text
  every(/Data/List[$T -> /Data/ToString], isa= [/Data/ToString])
    # A [List] whose elements are [ToString] is itself [ToString]: it renders as its items, each
      rendered in turn, separated by commas and wrapped in brackets — [[1, 2, 3]]. Declared on
      [List] (like [length] and [sum]) so any list type renders; the [ConsList] arms below
      implement it.

  :Nil.toString= "[]"
  :Cons[$T -> /Data/ToString](head@h, tail@t).toString =
    # [restToString] renders the items after the first, each with a leading ", " separator, so the
      opening item carries no comma and the commas fall between items. It destructures its own
      [head]/[tail], so the enclosing arm renames its fields to [h]/[t] to avoid the collision.
    restToString(lst -> ConsList[$T -> /Data/ToString]) -> String
    restToString(lst= Nil)= ""
    restToString(lst= Cons[$T -> /Data/ToString](head, tail))= ", " ++ head.toString ++ restToString(lst= tail)

    "[" ++ h.toString ++ restToString(lst= t) ++ "]"

  > [1, 2, 3]
    >>> [1, 2, 3]
  # ## Structural comparison helper
  consThen(first -> /Data/Algebra/Comparison, second -> /Data/Algebra/Comparison) -> /Data/Algebra/Comparison
    # [consThen] sequences the two comparisons a lexicographic ordering needs: the heads decide the
      order unless they are [Equal], in which case the tails' comparison ([second]) decides. The
      [compareTo] instance at the end of this file uses it.
  consThen(first= /Data/Algebra/Equal, second)= second
  consThen(first= /Data/Algebra/LessThan, second)= /Data/Algebra/LessThan
  consThen(first= /Data/Algebra/GreaterThan, second)= /Data/Algebra/GreaterThan

# # ConsList Functor instance
  A [ConsList] is a [Functor]: [fmap] applies a function to every element while preserving the
  list's shape — same length, same order — so mapping [f] over [[1, 2, 3]] gives [[f 1, f 2, f 3]].
  Lists are the canonical [Functor]; "map a function over a collection" is exactly the operation
  [fmap] generalises.
module(Data)
  every(/Data/List/ConsList[$T -> $_T], isa= [/Data/Functor])
module(Data/List)
  # [fmap] over a [ConsList] rebuilds the list, applying [fn] to each [head]. This is the [ConsList]
  # instance of the generic [fmap] declared over [Functor] in [Data/functor]. The instance is
  # written under the declaration's absolute name so the open [Functor] interface need not be
  # totally covered while still resolving for [fmap] calls on a [ConsList].
  /Data/Functor/fmap(lst= Nil, fn(v))= Nil
  /Data/Functor/fmap(lst= Cons(head, tail), fn(v))= Cons(head= fn(v= head), tail= /Data/Functor/fmap(lst= tail, fn(v)= fn(v= v)))

  > /Data/Functor/fmap(lst= [1, 2, 3], fn(v)= v + 1)
    >>> [2, 3, 4]

# # ConsList Eq membership
  Makes a [ConsList] of any [Eq] element a proper member of [Eq], so the generic [operator==]
  dispatches through the [equal] method. Two lists are equal when they match constructor for
  constructor with equal heads pairwise; the recursion runs through [tail.equal]. This is the
  idiomatic path (vs. a standalone operator overload), and mirrors Haskell's `instance Eq a => Eq
  [a]`. The element bound `$T -> Eq` makes the membership conditional on the element being [Eq], so
  the head comparison on the elements typechecks.
module(Data)
  every(/Data/List/ConsList[$T -> /Data/Algebra/Eq], isa= [/Data/Algebra/Eq])
module(Data/Algebra)
  :/Data/List/Nil.equal(other= /Data/List/Nil)= True
  :/Data/List/Nil.equal(other= /Data/List/Cons(head, tail))= False
  :/Data/List/Cons(head, tail).equal(other= /Data/List/Nil)= False
  :/Data/List/Cons[$T -> /Data/Algebra/Eq](head@ah, tail@at).equal(other= /Data/List/Cons(head@bh, tail@bt))= (ah == bh) && at.equal(other= bt)
module(Data/List)
  # Equal lists compare equal element-wise, and lists that differ in an element or in length do
  #   not. The element [Eq] dispatch is generic, so lists of [Integer], [Boolean], etc. all work.
  > ([1, 2] == [1, 2])
    >>> True
  > ([1, 2] == [1, 3])
    >>> False
  > ([1, 2] == [1])
    >>> False

# # ConsList Ord membership
  Makes a [ConsList] of any [Ord] element a proper member of [Ord], so [compareTo] dispatches per
  constructor. Lists are ordered lexicographically ([consThen] sequences the head comparison with
  the tail's); the recursion runs through [tail.compareTo]. Mirrors the [Eq] membership above (and
  every [Ord] is an [Eq], which the [Eq] membership already supplies).
module(Data)
  every(/Data/List/ConsList[$T -> /Data/Algebra/Ord], isa= [/Data/Algebra/Ord])
module(Data/Algebra)
  :/Data/List/Nil.compareTo(other= /Data/List/Nil)= /Data/Algebra/Equal
  :/Data/List/Nil.compareTo(other= /Data/List/Cons(head, tail))= /Data/Algebra/LessThan
  :/Data/List/Cons(head, tail).compareTo(other= /Data/List/Nil)= /Data/Algebra/GreaterThan
  :/Data/List/Cons[$T -> /Data/Algebra/Ord](head@ah, tail@at).compareTo(other= /Data/List/Cons(head@bh, tail@bt))= /Data/List/consThen(first= ah.compareTo(other= bh), second= at.compareTo(other= bt))
module(Data/List)
  # Lists order lexicographically: the first differing element decides, and a prefix is ordered
  #   before its extension ([Nil] before any [Cons]).
  > [1].compareTo(other= [2]).isLess
    >>> True
  > [1].compareTo(other= [1, 2]).isLess
    >>> True
  > [1, 2].compareTo(other= [1, 2]).isEq
    >>> True

# # ConsList Monad instance
  [mmap] over a [ConsList] is concatMap: the function returns a whole list for each element, and
  the results are appended in order.
module(Data/List)
  # [append] joins two lists in order — the recursive structural join (it recurses through itself
  # so the recursion stays a concrete arrow).
  append(a -> ConsList[$T -> $_T], b -> ConsList[$T -> $_T]) -> ConsList[$T -> $_T]
  append(a= Nil, b)= b
  append(a= Cons(head, tail), b)= Cons(head= head, tail= append(a= tail, b= b))
module(Data)
  every(/Data/List/ConsList[$T -> $_T], isa= [/Data/Monad])
module(Data/List)
  # The [ConsList] instance of the generic [mmap] declared over [Monad] in [Data/monad]. Like the
  # [fmap] instance above, it is written under the declaration's absolute name so the open [Monad]
  # class is not required to be totally covered here.
  /Data/Monad/mmap(m= Nil, fn(v))= Nil
  /Data/Monad/mmap(m= Cons(head, tail), fn(v))= append(a= fn(v= head), b= /Data/Monad/mmap(m= tail, fn(v)= fn(v= v)))

  # [append] joins two lists end to end.
  > /Data/List/append(a= [1], b= [2])
    >>> [1, 2]
  # [mmap] over a [ConsList] is concatMap: the function returns a whole list per element and the
  #   results are appended in order, so a function ignoring its element repeats a constant list and
  #   one reading it can grow the list. Binding the empty list yields the empty list.
  > /Data/Monad/mmap(m= [1, 2], fn(v)= [0])
    >>> [0, 0]
  > /Data/Monad/mmap(m= [1, 2], fn(v)= [v, v])
    >>> [1, 1, 2, 2]
  > /Data/Monad/mmap(m= [], fn(v)= [v])
    >>> []
  # [pure] for [ConsList] builds a singleton list; the call site's expected list type selects
  # this instance (return-type-directed dispatch — see [pure] in [Data/monad]).
  /Data/Monad/pure[$M -> /Data/List/ConsList[$T -> $_T]](v)= Cons(head= v, tail= Nil)

  pureConsInt(v -> Integer) -> /Data/List/Cons..[$T -> Integer]
  pureConsInt(v)= /Data/Monad/pure(v= v)

  > pureConsInt(v= 1)
    >>> [1]

import "core"


# Tests the syntax view of the debugger: a definition written as intermediate lines leading to a
  result, with a line used twice, a line never used, a nested helper taking its own parameter, an
  [#assert] and a [#debug], a call to another top level function, an if and a bind.
scale(v -> Integer) -> Integer= v * 10

sign(x -> Integer) -> Integer= if(x >= 0)
  Then= 1

  Else= -1

total(a -> Integer, b -> Integer) -> Integer =
  sum= a + b

  unused= a * b

  helper(y -> Integer) -> Integer= y + sum

  #assert(test= sum >= 0)
  #debug(d= sum)
  scale(v= helper(y= sum)) + sum * sign(x= a)

bump(m -> /Data/Maybe[$T -> Integer]) -> /Data/Maybe =
  x<- m

  doubled= x + x

  /Data/Maybe/Some(value= doubled + 1)

# A map over a list with a function of this page, so a run has an fmap among the calls of a
  function, and under each element of the fmap the calls of a function written over several lines.
totals(xs -> /Data/List[$T -> Integer]) -> /Data/List[$T -> Integer] =
  shifted= fmap(lst= xs, fn(v)= total(a= v, b= 2))

  shifted

main{io -> IO} =
  #assert(test= bump(m= /Data/Maybe/Some(value= 5)) == /Data/Maybe/Some(value= 11))
  #assert(test= totals(xs= [1, 2]) == [63, 84])
  io.exit(val= total(a= 1, b= 2) - 63)
